prompt: Review an AI change-remediation agent. During a 2,000-case adversarial evaluation, 40 cases contain direct injection, 60 indirect injection, 100 poisoned-retrieval documents and 1,800 benign cases. The system blocks 38 direct, 51 indirect and 70 poisoned cases, but also blocks 90 benign cases. Of the 41 successful attacks, deterministic authorization stops 35 before any effect; approval stops 4 more; 2 create reversible test-namespace changes. A kill test starts with 24 queued actions: 18 are denied immediately, 4 finish before revocation reaches the tool broker and 2 remain unaccounted for. The model image has a digest and valid signature, but the verification policy does not constrain signer identity or issuer; the model file uses a code-executing serialization format. Raw prompts and access tokens are retained in decision logs for 365 days. Decide whether to promote, calculate the useful rates, and specify the minimum recovery and prevention work.
directAnswer: Do not promote. The detector blocks 159 of 200 adversarial cases, so attack detection recall is 79.5%; 41 evade it. It blocks 90 of 1,800 benign cases, a 5% benign false-positive rate, and precision among its 249 blocks is 159/249, about 63.86%. Layered enforcement contains 39 of 41 detector escapes before an effect, about 95.12%, but two reversible effects still violate the declared invariant. The kill path accounts for only 22 of 24 queued actions and permits four to finish, so containment is neither complete nor proven. Signature validity without expected signer/issuer policy is insufficient, safe provenance does not make a code-executing format safe, and raw tokens in year-long logs are an active disclosure risk.
foundation: Security evaluation must preserve denominators and distinguish detector quality from system-level harm prevention. A detector can miss attacks while deterministic authorization prevents effects; that is precisely why layers exist. Promotion still depends on the declared invariant and residual risk, not on averaging a detector score with control success. Signatures, provenance, serialization safety, audit privacy and kill-path accounting answer different questions.
reasoningSteps: Count adversarial cases: 40+60+100=200. Blocks are 38+51+70=159, so detector recall is 159/200=79.5% and detector escapes are 41/200=20.5%.
Benign false positives are 90/1800=5%. Total blocks are 159+90=249; precision is 159/249, approximately 63.86%. Report class definitions and confidence rather than calling one score security.
Of 41 detector escapes, authorization stops 35 and approval stops 4, so 39/41, approximately 95.12%, are contained before effect by those two layers. Two of 41, approximately 4.88%, produce effects.

Across all 200 attacks, two produce effects, an observed attack-to-effect rate of 1%. If the invariant is zero unauthorized changes, any such effect blocks promotion even when reversible and confined to a test namespace.
The direct detector recall is 38/40=95%; indirect is 51/60=85%; poisoned retrieval is 70/100=70%. The aggregate hides the weakest path.

Kill accounting is 18 denied + 4 completed = 22 known outcomes, leaving 2/24, or 8.33%, unaccounted. Four of 24, or 16.67%, complete after the kill begins. Measure timing from invocation to enforcement and reconcile every idempotency key.

A digest identifies bytes and a valid signature proves a cryptographic statement under some key. Admission must constrain expected artifact, signer identity, issuer, claims, provenance and trusted root. Neither evidence proves semantic safety.
A loader that can execute code must be isolated or replaced with an admitted safe format and parser. Do not load the artifact merely to scan it inside a trusted control-plane process.

Stop unsafe log capture, restrict and preserve only incident-required evidence, rotate exposed tokens, establish exposure scope, and move to structured decisions with handles, hashes, classifications, masking, access and retention.

Keep the candidate disabled. Repair the kill path, reconcile the two effects and two unknown actions, narrow tools and credentials, bind provenance policy, change serialization handling, fix log lifecycle, rerun system-level adversarial tests and obtain independent risk acceptance for remaining limitations.
seniorAnswer: Promotion is rejected. Detector recall is 79.5% overall, but only 70% for poisoned retrieval; 20.5% of attacks evade it. The benign false-positive rate is 5%, and block precision is about 63.86%. Authorization and approval contain 39 of 41 escapes, about 95.12%, demonstrating useful defense in depth, yet two unauthorized changes still occur. Under a zero-unauthorized-change invariant the observed 1% attack-to-effect rate fails the gate. The kill exercise is also failed: four actions finish after invocation and two remain unaccounted. I would deny the agent route, revoke its tool identity, reconcile all 24 idempotency keys and both test changes, and preserve sanitized evidence. I would require identity- and issuer-constrained signature/provenance verification, a non-code-executing admitted model format or isolated loader, and structured redacted decision logs with short justified retention; exposed tokens are rotated. Then I would rerun per-technique and system-level tests that observe downstream state, containment latency and complete queue accounting. Detector improvement is desirable, but deterministic least privilege, downstream authorization and recoverable control remain the primary harm boundaries.
weakAnswer: Promote because 99% of attacks cause no effect, the two changes are reversible, and the artifact is signed.
whyWeak: It ignores the zero-effect invariant, the weak poisoned-retrieval slice, unknown queued actions, post-kill completions, unconstrained signer policy, executable artifact format and credential leakage. Reversibility reduces impact; it does not authorize the effect.

followUps.prompt: Why not combine detector recall and authorization containment into one percentage?
followUps.answer: They have different denominators and answer different questions. Detector recall measures labeled attacks caught at one layer; containment measures what happened to detector escapes. Keeping them separate reveals dependence and where improvements are needed.

Signing can bind bytes to an identity and protect integrity after signing. It does not prove the signer was authorized, the training data was clean, the model is behaviorally safe or the serialization format cannot execute code.

followUps.prompt: What should a red-team pass criterion observe?
followUps.answer: The protected system invariant and downstream state: for example, no unauthorized commit, no cross-tenant disclosure, complete queue accounting and bounded kill latency—not merely whether the model printed a refusal.
